questionStem: A 27-year-old man comes to student health services because of a 6-week history of increasingly severe insomnia and persistent fatigue. During this time, he also has had feelings of guilt, emptiness, hopelessness, and profound sadness. He is a graduate student and has withdrawn from most social activity. He says that during the past 4 years he has heard "Sauron" from a fantasy novel instructi ng him to renounce his family and forswear all sexual activity. He notes that he has had two episodes of depressed mood during the past 2 years. He began sertraline therapy during the second episode and had improvement in his mood; he discontinued the therapy 6 months ago because he was feeling well apart from intermittent hallucinations. He has no other history of serious illness and currently takes no medicat ions. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examinat ion, he has a depressed mood and restricted affect. His thought processes are mildly tangential. He does not appear to be responding to internal stimuli. He has not had suicidal ideatio n. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?

choices.B: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

correctExplanation: According to the DSM-5, patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (eg, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder) demonstrate at least two of the following five symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms (eg, flat affect, apathy, alogia). Many patients also illustrate prodroma l periods of strange behavior and social withdrawal. To meet diagnostic criteria, patients must demonstrate functional deficits, and the total duration of symptoms must exceed 6 months. Patients with schizoaffective disorder must demonstrate mood episodes (eg, major depressive episodes as in this patient, manic episodes) for a substantial portion of the duration of the illness. Major depressive episodes include depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or feelings of worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, suicidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). However, patients with schizoaffective disorder must also experience psychotic symptoms (eg, delusions, hallucinations) in the absence of mood symptoms for at least 2 weeks. Management requires antipsychotic medication and may also include adjunctive antidepressant medication (if depressive episodes are predominant) or mood stabilizer medication (if manic episodes are predominant).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dysthymic disorder (Choice A), more commonly known as persistent depressive disorder, refers to depressive symptoms lasting longer than 2 years. Patients with dysthymic disorder do not meet major depressive disorder criteria (as in this patient) and do not typically demonstrate psychotic symptoms. \ j - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - •

questionStem: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician for evaluation of difficulty reading. His teache r reports that he cannot keep up with his classmates. His mother reports that he is genera lly well behaved but frequently flaps his hands when he is nervous. Physical exam ination shows a high forehead, prominent supraorbital ridges, protruding ears, and a prominent jaw. Psychoed ucational testing of the patient shows an IQ of 65. Academ ic achievement testing is consistent with his IQ. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.B: Decreased numbers of trinucleotide repeats of the X chromosome
choices.C: Decreased serum hypoxanth ine phosphoribosy ltransfe rase activity
choices.D: Fragile site on the X chromosome
choices.E: Increased expression of the homeobox A 1 (HOXA 1) gene
choices.F: Increased serum concentratio ns of phenylpyruv ic acid
choices.G: Increased serum concentratio ns of pyruvate

correctExplanation: This patient's constellation of findings, including intellectual disabi lity, an elongated face, and large ears, is suggestive of fragile X syndrome. Patients may also present with macroorchidism, hyperextensible joints, and a high-arched palate. Fragile X syndrome is the second most common cause of inherited intellectual disability after Down syndrome and is inherited in an X-linked dominant fashion. It is caused by a CGG-trinucleotide repeat expansion within the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. On karyotype, the end of the X chromosome appears truncated, leading to the name fragile X syndrome. Patients with fragile X syndrome are at increased risk for mitral valve prolapse and educational difficulties. They are often diagnosed with autism. As with all trinucleotide repeat expansions, genetic anticipation is seen, wherein future generations have increased severity and/or earlier onset of disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Congenital rubella (Choice A) presents in newborns with the classic triad of cataracts, sensorineura l deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus. It is unlikely to be a cause of intellectual disability presenting in childhood. Increased, not decreased (Choice B), numbers of trinucleotide repeats of the X chromosome are seen in fragile X syndrome. Decreased serum hypoxanthine phosphoribosy ltransferase activity (Choice C) is seen in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. questionStem: A 28-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of flu-like symptoms and cough productive of clear sputum for 24 hours. He has been hospitalized eight times over the past 5 years because of bizarre delusions and hallucinations during which a voice tells him what to do. He has a 9-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus. In addition to insulin, he is receiving clozapi ne therapy (400 mg daily) for his psychotic condition. During mental status examination, he is hallucinating and says that h,e is being pursued by special agents of the government. Leukocyte count is 2750/mm 3, and serum glucose concentration is 140 mg/dl. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: This patient's leukopenia may be related to agranulocytosis, a rare but life-threatening adverse effect of clozapine therapy that leads to increased susceptibility to infection. The pathogenesis may be related to the production of reactive oxygen species in the bone marrow. Patients on clozapine therapy must have their absolute neutrophil count monitored regularly. In suspected clozapine-induced agranulocytosis, clozapine should be discontinued. Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic medication effective in treatment- refractory schizophrenia. Though clozapine carries a lower risk than many antipsychotics of causing extrapyramidal symptoms, clozapine is associated with serious adverse effects such as agranulocytosis, myocarditis, and seizure. Clozapine may also lead to severe sedation and constipation (as a result of its anticholinergic activity) along with sialorrhea (potentially also related to modulation of acetylcholine signaling).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adding lithium carbonate therapy (Choice A) would be ineffective in acute agranulocytosis. In patients who experience agranulocytosis but require clozapine for psychiatric stability, physicians may choose to rechallenge patients with clozapine. During a clozapine rechallenge specifically, adjunctive lithium may mitigate clozapine-related myelosuppression. Adding penicillin therapy (Choice B) would be premature in this patient without a diagnosed bacterial infection. His symptoms may be attributable to a viral upper respiratory infection. Decreasing the dose of clozapine (Choice C) would be insufficient to allow the recovery of leukocyte counts. Clozapine should be discontinued.

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because "he does whatever he wants and comes and goes as he pleases." They report that he always has been challenging to manage and has not respon ded to disciplinary measures since he was 10 years of age. During the past 2 years, his behavior has become worse; he has been arrested twice in the past month, once for assault and once for vanda lism. He is current ly on probation. His parents state that they have found him intoxicated in his room on several occasions, and they recently found marijuana paraphernalia in his room. Today, the patient is sullen and minimally cooperative. He says he is frequently irritable and short tempered . His clothes smell of cigarette smoke. Physical examination shows severa l tattoos over the chest and upper extremities and several body piercings; no other abnormalities are noted . Mental status examination shows an irritab le mood and poor eye contact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Conduct disorder refers to persistent emotiona l and behavioral problems such as purposefu l aggression toward people and animals in children and adolescents. The behavioral problems can also include theft, lying, destruction of property, and serious rule violations. The diagnosis of conduct disorder can be given in children with repetitive and pervasive patterns of violating major societal norms, rules, and basic rights of others. Children with conduct disorder are at increased risk for developing antisocial personality disorder as an adult. Treatment for both conduct disorder and antisocia l personality disorder includes psychotherapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Antisocial personality disorder (Choice A) is a cluster B personality disorder that arises from a deficit in empathy, resulting in pervasive violations of others' rights, aggression, and a hostile and manipulative attitude toward others. These patients may also be chronically bored and hence sensation seeking, leading to a high rate of substance abuse and gambling. It is generally diagnosed in adults, whereas the preferred diagnosis in children and adolescents is conduct disorder. Bipolar disorder (Choice B) is characterized by discrete episodes of depression and mania, which can sometimes be accompanied by psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions. -. . . - • • • • • . . -.

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of progressive headaches that have caused him to miss several days of school. They now occur daily and are always present on awakening in the morning. He describes the headaches as a diffuse, constant pressure that occasionally throbs. He feels better after taking acetaminophen and resting in front of the television for 10 to 20 minutes. He has not noticed any particular events that cause the headaches, and he says that they are not exacerbated by light, sound, coughing, or straining. He has not had nausea or vomiting. Two months ago, he sustained a whiplash injury in a motor vehicle collision. His parents say that he snores loudly. His mother and maternal aunt have migraines, and his father has major depressive disorder. The patient is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (189 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m2. He breathes throug h his mouth. Respirations are 20/min. Examination shows 3 to 5 beats of jerk nystagmus with far lateral gaze bilateral ly. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's headaches?
correctExplanation: Headaches that occur in the morning, resolve minutes to hours after awakening, have a pressure or squeezing type quality, and an absence of other symptoms are frequently reported by patients with untreated obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This patient is likely experiencing sleep-related hypoventilation caused by OSA. Clinical features of untreated OSA include excessive daytime fatigue, falling asleep at inappropriate times, loud snoring, and a disrupted sleep-wake cycle. Risk factors include male sex, obesity, congenital or traumatic anatomic abnormalities of the oropharynx and upper airway, neuromuscular disorders, and use of sedating medications. Untreated OSA is associated with hypertension. Management consists of lifestyle changes (weight loss, dietary modifications, increased activity, changing sleep position), avoiding sedating medications and substances, and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) while sleeping. Second-line therapies include oral appliances such as mandibular advancement devices for symptoms refractory to CPAP use, and surgery for cases with obstructing lesions of the airway.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hydrocephalus (Choice A) refers to abnormal enlargement of the ventricles and subarachnoid space caused by cerebrospina l fluid (CSF) accumulation, which may be a result of increased CSF production, decreased CSF absorption, or obstruction of CSF flow. Patients present with findings caused by increased intracranial pressure, which include headache, nausea, papilledema on retinal examination, ataxia, and encephalopathy. Severely increased pressure results in the Cushing triad of bradycardia, widened pulse ressure and h ertension, and irre ular breathin .

questionStem: A 24-year-o ld woman reports a 3-week history of recurrent fevers. She has a 4-year history of major depress ive disorder. Her temperature is 42°C (107.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion is otherwise normal. Her leukocyte count is 7500/mm 3 with a normal differential. Liver functio n tests and serum creatine kinase activity are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in patient care?

choices.C: Obtain a rectal temperature under supervision
choices.E: Order a CT scan of the abdomen

correctExplanation: In factitious disorder, patients consciously produce symptoms (eg, purposely injure themselves, fake a fever by eating something warm) for primary gain. Primary gain is the motivation to be cared for, which constitutes an unconscious motivator for the patient's conscious production of symptoms. Early losses, neglect, or abuse may disrupt patients ' identity and relationships, and adopting the sick role may represent patients ' attempts to cope with stress and stabilize their identity and relationships. Psychiatric comorbidities (eg, depression, substance use disorders, personality disorders) are common but not present in all patients. Diagnosis is supported by inconsistencies in the history or physical examination and a history of extensive clinical evaluations. This patient's isolated, severe hyperthermia without other associated vital sign changes (eg, tachycardia, hyper- or hypotension, and/or tachypnea) or physical examination or laboratory evidence of severe hyperthermia (eg, acute distress, diaphoresis, flushed skin, sequela of rhabdomyolysis such as increased creatinine or creatine kinase) is likely attributable to factitious disorder. To exclude a true fever and assist in establishing the factitious disorder diagnosis, a rectal temperature may be obtained in this patient. Treatment includes regular follow-up with one physician who oversees management (as opposed to symptom-triggered appointments) and possible psychotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Administering broad-spectrum antibiotics (Choice A) or ordering a CT scan of the abdomen (Choice E) are likely unnecessary in this patient without focal infectious symptoms or vital signs indicative of sepsis physiology (eg, tachycardia and hypotension). The patient's temperature should be confirmed before evaluating or treating for infectious causes. Administering corticosteroids (Choice B) may treat recurrent fevers related to rare autoimmune or autoinflammatory conditions. However, it has not yet been established that the patient has a true fever, and this patient does not demonstrate other evidence of autoimmune disease on history or physical examination.

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of fatigue, insomnia, and anxiety. His divorce was finalized 1 month ago, ending his 10-year marriage to his wife, who he learned was having an affair with his best friend. He feels anger toward his ex-wife and his friend, but he says, "I know what they did was wrong and that I am a good person who got hurt by them." He has no regrets about the divorce because he believes that he never would have been able to trust her again. He is relieved that they have no children. He often thinks about whether he will remar ry, which causes anxiety and prevents him from sleeping. He has had no change in appetite. He works as a middle school teacher and has missed several days of school because of tiredness. His mind wanders when he watches television or reads at home. He has decreased energy but still enjoys activities with family and friends . He has no history of medical or psychiatric illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within norma l limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On menta l status examination, he is cooperative and engaging and exhibits a full range of affect. He says that his mood is okay. His thoughts are organized. There is no evidence of suicida l or homicidal ideation . Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Adjustment disorder refers to the onset of an emotional disturbance within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. The emotiona l disturbance manifests as marked distress out of proportion to the stressor and a significant impairment in daily functioning. Adjustment disorders are typically associated with anxiety, depression, or behavioral symptoms without meeting the criteria for anxiety or depressive disorders. For example, this patient demonstrates some neurovegetative symptoms (eg, decreased sleep and energy) and trouble concentrating but not depressed mood or anhedonia. As adjustment disorder is typica lly self-limited, the treatment of adjustment disorder commonly includes brief supportive psychotherapy, though brief pharmacotherapy that targets associated anxiety or depressive symptoms may also be empirically provided. In young patients with severe insomnia and without substance use disorders, nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic medications (eg, zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) may be appropriate. Given that nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic medications increase the risk for falls, sedation, cognitive impairment, and addiction, these medications should be used with caution in older patients and patients with substance use disorders.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Fluoxetine (Choice A) is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor used as a long-term medication for depression and anxiety disorders. It takes weeks to be effective. This patient's adjustment disorder symptoms will likely be self-limited and/or respond to brief pharmacotherapy.

questionStem: One month after undergo ing liver transp lantation, a 4 7-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital for treatment of organ rejection . Twenty-four hours after intravenous methylprednisolone therapy is begun, she begins to have visual hallucinations that her organ donor has entered her hospita l room naked and is drawing symbols on her skin with an eyebrow pencil. Current medications include tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, omeprazo le, trimethoprim-s ulfamethoxazo le, acyclov ir, and nystatin. The patient has no history of psychiatric illness. She is awake and alert. Physical examination shows a well-healing surgical incision over the abdomen. On mental status examination, she says she is worried about her visual hallucinations. She is oriented to person, place, and time. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's psychiatric symptoms?
correctExplanation: Systemic corticosteroids have many adverse effects, including neuropsychiatric effects such as psychosis and mood disorders. These adverse effects are usually reversible with reduction of dosing, although some require treatment. Psychosis describes an episode in which a patient may experience delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought and speech, and agitation or hyperarousal. It may be caused by a primary psychiatric disorder (eg, schizophrenia), a primary medical condition, or substance use, including medications. Common causes of substance-induced psychosis include alcohol, anticholinergics, antiparkinsonian medications, and corticosteroids. This patient without a psychiatric history is experiencing visual hallucinations in the context of recent corticosteroid exposure, making corticosteroid-induced psychotic disorder the most likely explanation for her symptoms.

Delirium (Choice C) is an acute confusional state typically associated with acute medical illness in older patients. Delirium presents with acute disturbances in awareness, attention, and baseline cognition that fluctuate in severity over the course of the day. questionStem: A 42-year-o ld man comes to the physician for a routine examination. He is accompanied by his wife. During the examination, his wife states that he is competitive, rigid, stubborn, and opinionated. She feels he has difficulty making simple decisions and discarding old items that are of no use and is anxious and obsessed with being early for everything. He is a successful lawyer, and his coworkers have said that he believes that his way is the only way of getting things done. When asked about this, he does not think there is a problem. Examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is a cluster C personality disorder, the anxious or fearful cluster. It is characterized by excessively rigid routines and perfectionism. Patients often display an obsession with control and the belief that their approach to a specific problem or situation is the only correct approach. A patient 's family, friends, or coworkers often note rigid, stubborn thought patterns. This rigidity and obsession with perfection may occur at the expense of a patient's social relationships or career, as evidenced by this patient's difficulty making simple decisions. Patients with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder do not display intrusive, recurrent thoughts or compulsive behaviors as seen in obsessive-compulsive disorder, which is an anxiety disorder, not a personality disorder. Personality disorders are persistently maladaptive ways of relating to the self and to society that typically appear by early adulthood.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice A) features excessive and persistent worrying that may be associated with sympathetic hyperactivity. Patients do not typically display excessive orderliness, rigidity, or perfectionism. Narcissistic personality disorder (Choice B) is a cluster B personality disorder, the emotional or dramatic cluster, that is characterized by fragile self-esteem and compensatory arrogant, self-aggrandizing behavior to gain admiration, sometimes at others' expense. Panic disorder (Choice D) features acute fear or anxiety that peaks within minutes and is associated with symptoms of sympathetic hyperactivity such as tachycardia, heart palpitations, sweating, and trembling along with shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, gastrointestina l distress, and paresthesias. Panic disorder is characterized by recurrent panic attacks that are unexpected and associated with worry about future panic attacks or avoidance of panic attack triggers.

questionStem: A 24-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department from a psychiatr ic hospita l because of a decreasing level of consciousness over the past 3 days. He has become progress ively less responsive and has rema ined in bed for the past 12 hours without speak ing or following commands. He has a history of schizophrenia with multip le psychiatric hospita lizations and is current ly being treated with haloperidol and benztropine. His tempera ture is 39.4 °C (103°F), pulse is 120/min, resp irations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg. He withdraws weak ly to noxious stimuli. His eyes are open, but he does not fix or follow visual stimuli or gaze around the room . He is mute and does not follow commands. Exami nation shows marked rigidity of the neck and all extremities. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 18,000/mm 3 Segmented neutrophils 80% Lymphocytes 20% Serum creatine kinase 12,000 U/L Cerebrospina l fluid Erythrocyte count Leukocyte count Protein Glucose 2/mm 3 1/mm 3 28 mg/dL 78 mg/dL A CT scan of the head shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

NMS is a life-th reaten ing condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. Common causative agents are antipsychotics (especially high-potency antipsychotics such as haloperido l) and antidopaminergic nausea medications. Rigidity results from dopamine antagonism in the nigrostriatal pathway, while autonomic dysfunction and hyperthermia may result from dopamine antagonism in the hypothalamus. questionStem: A 57-year-o ld woman comes to the phys ician because of difficulty sleeping, tearf ulness, and restless ness since her daughte r was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer 3 days ago. She reports that when she goes to bed at night, she is unable to fall asleep for several hours and lays in bed worry ing about her daughter's situation. The patient underwe nt a mastectomy for breast cancer 7 years ago. She takes acetaminophen /butalbital for occasiona l migraines. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she is tearf ul and tense but calms during the conversat ion. There is no evidence of suicida l ideat ion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by friends 20 minutes after the onset of bizarre behavior that began at a party. His friends say that he became paranoid and started threate ning them. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Physical examination shows agitation, diaphoresis, horizontal nystagmus , and occasional myoclonus. Mental status examination shows dysarthric speech and combativeness. His thoughts are disorganized, and he is unable to give a coherent history. He believes that the physician is trying to kill him. Thirty minutes later, he becomes somnolent. Administration of naloxone does not improve his condition. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Phencyclidine, also known as PCP, is an NMDA glutamatergic receptor antagonist that is used recreationally for its euphoria-inducing and dissociative effects. PCP intoxication is often characterized by signs and symptoms including hyperthermia, hypertension, tachycardia, erratic behavior, paranoia, psychosis, aggression, decreased sensation, ataxia, nystagmus, myoclonus, and dysarthria. Patients may require sedation, treatment with antipsychotic medications, or physical restraint until their symptoms subside. Withdrawa l symptoms following PCP intoxication are uncommon. Naloxone has no effect on the pathways involved in PCP intoxication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alcohol intoxication (Choice A) presents with sedation, altered mentation, dysarthria, and vomiting. Alcohol withdrawal may lead to severe complications including delirium tremens and seizures. Alcoho l intoxication does not typically present with nystagmus; hyperthermia and autonomic instability would also be uncommon in acute intoxication, though the vasodepressive and sedating effects can result in hypotension and bradypnea. Amphetamine intoxication (Choice B) may resemb le PCP intoxication and also presents with hyperthermia, hypertension, tachycardia, erratic behavior, and paranoid or delusional thinking. However, it does not typically present with nystagmus, ataxia, or myoclonus. Opioid intoxication (Choice C) may result in erratic behavior, miosis, respiratory depression, and obtundation but should respond rapidly to administration of naloxone. Failure of respiratory depression and mental status to improve following naloxone administration should lead to consideration of alternative diagnoses.

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of increasing distress about his procrast ination and indecision. He has been late for work often because he is easily distracted by any task; as a result, he has received poor job performance ratings. He arrived late for today's examination because he was awake late last night creating a new computer folder system and then had to refold the clothes in his closet several times this morning. He says he becomes nervous if he is unable to finish similar minor projects. He somet imes daydreams about projects and must complete them in his daydreams before attending to other tasks . He reports that his family is exasperated by his behavior. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He appears fatigued. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. On mental status exam ination, he is fully oriented. He is cooperative but fidgets and has poor eye contact. He is able to repeat six digits forwa rd, spell "world" backward, and perform serial sevens. He gives four interpretations of a proverb and is unable to decide on a final answer. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) manifests as recurrent, iintrusive urges or thoughts (obsessions) that the patient tries to relieve or neutralize by repetitive rituals (compulsions). These symptoms are time-consuming and cause significant anxiety to the patient and markedly impair functioning. Compulsions can occur in response to a fear of "incompleteness, " which requires repetitive actions until a task is considered complete, as in this patient. Other common obsessive-compulsion symptoms are related to cleaning, symmetry, harm to self or others, and taboo thoughts or ideas. For example, a classic case of OCD is a patient with obsessions regarding cleanliness and contamination, whose compulsions include excessive bathing or hand washing. Patients with OCD also commonly experience anxiety or major mood disorders. It typical ly presents relatively early in life, with most cases present by age 20 years. It is common ly treated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, clomipramine, or venlafaxine, in addition to cognitive behavioral therapy.

It can persist into adulthood with similar symptoms but does not cause obsessions or compu lsions, as in this patient. Delusional disorder (Choice B) features the presence of one or more delusions for a month or longer without other schizophrenia symptoms. Prominent obsession and compu lsions would be atypical of delusional disorder. questionStem: A 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency departme nt by police after he was found wandering on the street. The officers say that the patient was screaming and talking to himself. He is unkempt and agitated , and he is wearing winter clothes on a hot summer day. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. During the examination, he says that he is not going to take any medicine, and the "television told me about the murders." Which of the following is the most likely additional finding in this patient?

choices.A: Cerebra l edema o n CT scan of the head
choices.B: Enlarged lateral and third ventricles on CT scan of the head
choices.C: Increased serum dopam ine concentratio n
choices.D: Increased serum and urine copper concentrations

correctExplanation: According to the DSM-5, patients with schizophrenia demonstrate at least two of the following five symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms (eg, flat affect, apathy, alogia). Many patients also illustrate prodromal periods of strange behavior and social withdrawal. To meet diagnostic criteria, patients must demonstrate functiona l deficits, and the total duration of symptoms must exceed 6 months. In recent decades, schizophrenia has been postulated to result from excessive pruning of glutamatergic synapses in the cerebral cortex during critical periods of development, explaining the negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia (glutamatergic hypofunction may then dysregu late mesolimbic dopamine to produce the positive symptoms of schizophrenia). As a result of synapse loss and neurona l atrophy in the cortex, enlarged lateral and third ventricles may be demonstrated on neuroimaging. Treatment requires antipsychotic medications.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cerebral edema on CT scan of the head (Choice A) arises from a variety of causes including trauma, ischemic stroke, intracranial masses, and hydrocepha lus. Cerebral edema does not typical ly occur in schizophrenia. Increased serum dopamine concentration (Choice C) is unlikely, since dopamine increases in schizophrenia are specific to certain regions of the brain only (eg, mesolimbic pathway). Dopamine in the central nervous system (CNS) does not cross the blood-brain barrier to the systemic vasculature. Increased serum and urine copper concentrations (Choice D) are typical of Wilson disease. Wilson disease is a rare condition of copper accumulation throughout the body (including the CNS) and may present with psychosis. This patient lacks other signs of Wilson disease such as liver disease or ocular findings, and primary psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia are more common.

questionStem: A 42-year-o ld woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of a 5-month history of increasi ngly severe episodes of lower abdominal pain. The pain is exacerbated during bowel movements, sexual intercourse, and menses. Treatment with several analgesics has not controlled the pain. Laparoscopy 4 years ago and a second laparoscopy 2 years ago for evaluation of pain showed no abnorma lities. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they use condoms for contraception. She is a single parent and lost her job 6 months ago. She now has difficulty sleeping 1 to 3 nights each week because she worries about finding a job. Abdom inal examination shows tenderness in both lower quadrants. Pelvic examination shows a mobile, nontender uterus and normal, nontender adnexa. A complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentat ion rate, Pap smear, and urine and cervical cultures show no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determ ine the cause of this patient's pain?
correctExplanation: Somatic symptom disorder, formerly referred to as somatoform disorder, is the most likely cause of this patient's pain with ongoing symptoms despite an extensive evaluation and may be diagnosed on psychiatric assessment. According to the DSM-5, patients with somatic symptom disorder are preoccupied with an existing somatic symptom such that these symptoms disrupt the patient's daily life. These symptoms may or may not originate from an underlying illness, though they are typically unconsciously produced or exacerbated by psychological factors such as stress, as in this patient. Patients with somatic symptom disorder persistently devote excessive time and energy to these symptoms or related health concerns (eg, repeatedly going to the doctor). Somatic symptom disorder typically demonstrates a chronic and fluctuating course. Management of somatic symptom disorder centers around regular primary care follow­ up that targets coping skills, provides reassurance, and avoids unnecessary tests.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. MRI of the pelvis (Choice A) is unlikely to demonstrate a cause of this patient's pain. While it may be used to evaluate causes such as infection or malignancy, this patient has been extensively evaluated. This patient's symptoms are likely secondary to somatic symptom disorder, which warrants a psychiatric assessment. Hysteroscopy (Choice C) allows visualization of the uterine cavity and is useful in diagnosing endometrial polyps or structural abnormalities. This patient's physical examination and previous laparoscopies did not show evidence of any structural abnormalities that would explain her symptoms.

questionStem: A 14-yea r-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of poor academic performance since her family relocated to a new town 6 months ago. The patient is halfway through the eighth grade a nd has been earning mostly D's and F's in school. She is having trouble making friends, especia lly since she lost her place on the school track team because of her poor academic performance. In her last school, she earned mostly A's and B's and had many friends. The family moved after the sudden death of the patient's father as a result of a motor vehicle collision in which the patient was a passenger. The patient had sustained minor injuries that were successf ully treated. Since the family moved, she has been having frequent nightmares, is easily startled, and has trouble concentrating. Her mother says that her daughter seems to be "walking around in a cloud" much of the time. Physical examination shows no abnormal ities. On mental status examination, the patient fidgets and is somew hat slow to respond to questions. She is oriented to person, place, and time. She says she feels nervous all of the time. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a syndrome of psychological consequences of direct or witnessed exposure to serious physical or sexual violence or trauma. Though some patients recover quickly from traumatic events, vulnerable patients may develop PTSD. Patients with PTSD experience intrusive thoughts/memories (eg, nightmares or flashbacks), dysregulation of arousal (eg, restlessness, nervousness, easy startle, decreased concentration), avoidance of reminders, and negative mood/thoughts (eg, psychomotor retardation, feelings of detachment). To meet diagnostic criteria for PTSD, these symptoms must last longer than 1 month and cause social or occupational dysfunction. Treatment typically includes psychotherapy (eg, exposure therapy) and/or antidepressant medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute stress disorder (Choice A) refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts, hyperarousal, dissociation, avoidance, and/or negative mood/thoughts that occur within 1 month of a traumatic event such as a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. This patient has been symptomatic for more than 1 month. Adjustment disorder (Choice B) refers to the onset of an emotional disturbance within 3 months of an identifiab le stressor, manifesting as marked distress out of proportion to the stressor and a significant impairment in daily functioning. By definition, patients with adjustment disorder do not meet criteria for other anxiety disorders, and this patient meets diagnostic criteria for PTSD.

questionStem: A 27-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after cutting her arms superficially with a razor blade. On arrival, she appears calm and is holding a stuffed animal. She says that she cut herse lf because she wanted to "feel something" and is unsure if she will be able to stop herself from doing this again. She says that she sleeps 8 hours each night and has a good appet ite. From the ages of 10 to 15 years , she was physica lly and sexual ly abused by her stepfather and mother on severa l occas ions. She has never had a long-term relationsh ip and has been fired from several jobs because of difficulty getting along with her superv isors. Her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows lacerations over both forearms . Neurologic examinat ion shows no abnormalities. On menta l status examination , she denies depressed mood or suicidal ideation but is convinced that she is worthless and deserves to die. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a cluster B personality disorder, the emotional or dramatic cluster, that features an unstable sense of self and tumultuous relationships. Likely caused by a combina tion of genetic polymorphisms in serotonin and dopamine receptors and emotional invalidation or abuse during childhood, patients with BPD unconsciously learn to make impulsive and dramatic gestures, including self-harm , to obtain attention and emotional fulfilment from others. As a result of inadequate emotional attunement from caregivers, patients with BPD do not learn to label, understand, or regulate their emotions. Their negative emotional experiences are so intensely painful that people with BPD must separate these experiences from their consciousness. This splitting leads people with BPD to black-and-white thinking that includes seeing people as all good or all bad. Because of affective dysfunction and hypodopaminergic tone, patients may use substances or self-harm (producing endorphins) to artificial ly create a positive affect. Chronic invalidation also leads to poor self-esteem (eg, worthlessness) and the consequent reliance on others for self-esteem needs, resulting in an intense fear of abandonment and severe distress when abandonment happens. The inability to self-soothe and difficulty being alone commonly leads to attachment to transitional objects (eg, stuffed animals).
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Conversion disorder (Choice B), also known as functional neurological disorder, involves neurologic symptoms such as sensory or ·

questionStem: An 87-year-o ld man is adm itted to the hospital because of dehydrat ion and emaciation. He appears catatonic and is unrespons ive to questions. One month ago, he began withdraw ing from relatives and talking constant ly about death. He gradually stopped eating and drinking and has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss during this time. He has a 35-year history of major depress ive disorder and has attempted suicide twice. He has no chron ic medical conditions and current ly takes no medications. He appears cachect ic and is staring into space. He does not respond to verbal stimuli. He is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m2. Exami nation shows tem poral wasting. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.D: Desipram ine and risper idone therapy

correctExplanation: Catatonia is a syndrome of severe psychomotor disturbances, classically characterized by immobility, mutism, stupor, staring, and absent responses to questions and instructions (negativism). It is frequently associated with an underlying psychiatric or general medical disorder. Delayed diagnosis can lead to poor outcomes. This patient displays evidence of severe malnutrition related to catatonia in the setting of major depressive disorder. He should be admitted to the hospital and treated promptly with a benzodiazepine or electroconvulsive therapy. Fluid resuscitation, electrolyte repletion, and careful monitoring of laboratory studies for refeeding syndrome should be performed as well. Both benzodiazepine and electroconvulsive therapy are considered safe and effective in the treatment of catatonia. Once the acute catatonic episode has resolved, additional treatment for the patient's underlying major depressive disorder shou ld be initiated.

Desipramine therapy only (Choice B), fluoxetine therapy only (Choice C), desipramine and risperidone therapy (Choice D), and fluoxetine and risperidone therapy (Choice E) are incorrect, since management of the patient's acute catatonic state is the priority. questionStem: A 25-year-o ld primigravid woman at 16 weeks' gestation has had increased episodes of crying, difficulty falling asleep, decreased energy, and loss of appetite over the past 6 weeks. She has a history of recurrent major depressive disorder. Her family is concerned that she might inadvertently harm herself or her fetus. Her husband reports that she has lost interest in daily activities. She states that she has no suicidal thoughts. She is concerned about her ability to take care of a newbo rn and is questioni ng her decision not to terminate the pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Reassurance with return visit in 2 weeks
choices.B: Explanation of the risks and benefits of antidepressant therapYi
choices.C: Explanation of the risks and benefits of therape utic abortion

correctExplanation: This patient meets criteria for major depressive disorder (MOD). Symptoms of MOD in pregnancy include 2 or more weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, suicidal or infanticidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. It is recommended that patients with recurrent major depressive episodes be treated with antidepressant medication indefinitely. In gravid patients with moderate to severe depressive symptoms, selective serotonin inhibitors (SSRls) and psychotherapy are genera lly recommended, since the risks of untreated depression (eg, neglect, suicide, infanticide) typical ly outweigh the risk of fetal adverse effects related to antidepressant medications. SSRls are not considered major teratogens, though third trimester use may lead to mild neonatal adjustment syndrome and, rarely, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. In gravid patients with MOD, physicians should discuss the risks and benefits of starting an SSRI medication versus not treating the MOD.

Patients with peripartum depression are at risk for suicide and infanticide and should be actively treated and monitored. A therapeutic abortion (Choice C) is performed to prevent mental or physical health complications. This patient's questioning of her decision not to terminate the pregnancy is likely the result, not the cause, of her MOD. Therefore, the physician should treat the patient's MOD before discussing a therapeutic abortion. Support group therapy (Choice D) is not a validated therapy for major depressive disorder. questionStem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of a 20-minute episode of severe chest pain and sweating that started 1 hour ago while he was watch ing television. On arrival, he is alert and repeated ly expresses concern that someth ing is "very wrong." He reports that during the episode, his heart was "pounding," he felt short of breath, and he was sure he was having a heart attack and was going to die. One month ago, he had a similar episode that occurred in the evening approximately 30 minutes after his high school football practice. At that time, results of laboratory studies and an ECG obtained in the emer,gency department showed no abnormalities. After the initial episode, he quit the footbal l team, and he has continued to limit his physical activity because he is afraid of bringing on another episode. He reports no insomnia or changes in appetite. His mother states that he was diagnosed with an innocent heart murmur at the age of 6 months, but it has not been noted on examinations since the age of 1 year. His paternal grandfather died of a myocard ial infarction 3 years ago at the age of 68 years. The patient takes no medications. He does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. He performs well in school. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 73 kg (161 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 130/83 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a normal S 1 and S2 with variation of S2 on respiration. The remainder of the exam ination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Panic disorder features panic attacks that occur unexpectedly and are associated with changes in behavior to avoid panic attack triggers. This patient is likely experiencing recurrent panic attacks consistent with panic disorder. Panic attacks feature acute fear or anxiety that peaks within minutes and is associated with four additiona l physical symptoms or associated mental states. These additional symptoms may include heart pa lpitations or tachycardia, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, the sensation of choking, gastrointestina l distress, paresthesias, sweating, chills, trembling, derealization, the fear of dying, and/or the fear of losing control. Panic disorder is a relatively common psychiatric disorder characterized by recurrent panic attacks that are unexpected and associated with worry about future panic attacks or avoidance of panic attack triggers. Treatment typical ly includes psychotherapy, long-term selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and short-term benzodiazepines.

questionStem: A 30-year-o ld law school graduate is caught cheating on the bar examinat ion. Further investigation shows previous allegations of cheating in junior high school and an adolescence characterized by occasiona l truancy, freque nt fights, and lying. As an adult, he has not been able to hold a job, has been bankrupt once, and was divorced because of failure to provide proper care for his children. He is angry about the accusation of cheating and insists that the incident is a misunderstanding. He has many friends. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Antisocial persona lity disorder is a cluster B persona lity disorder, the emotiona l or dramatic cluster, that arises from a deficit in empathy, resulting in pervasive violations of others' rights, aggression, and a hostile and manipulative attitude toward others. Similar to other cluster B personality disorders, patients with antisocial personality disorder struggle to regulate their emotions in that their frustration tolerance is low and they frequently behave impulsively. These patients may also be chronically bored and hence sensation seeking, leading to a high rate of substance use disorder and gambling. These personality traits lead to deficits in persona l (extreme ego­ centrism) and interpersonal (empathy, intimacy) functioning. Persona lity disorders are persistently maladaptive ways of relating to the self and to society that typica lly appear by early adulthood.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Borderline personality disorder (Choice B) is a cluster B personality disorder, the emotional or dramatic cluster, that features an unstable sense of self and tumultuous relationships. Patients may demonstrate splitting, and often have a history of self-harm (eg, cutting behavior). Patients with borderline personality disorder may experience transient psychosis when emotionally dysregu lated; delusions and hallucinations are atypical. Dissociative fugue (Choice C) is characterized by discrete episodes of amnesia, including loss of one's identity, in association with sudden travel or bewildered wandering. Dysthymic disorder (Choice D), also known as persistent depressive disorder, is characterized by signs and symptoms of depression that do not meet criteria for major depressive disorder and which occur on most days over a period of at least 2 years. questionStem: A 37-year-o ld male police officer comes to the physician at the request of his superiors 1 week after he witnessed a terrorist bombing during which several civilians and three fe llow police officers were killed. He sustained only minor injuries and assisted in rescuing survivors and gathering body parts. Since the bombing, he has felt emotionally numb and has been unable to enjoy activities he used to find pleasurab le. He has continued to work but has requested assignments far removed from the site of the attack. He describes his sleep as fitful. Two years ago, he sustained a bullet wound to the right calf, which left him with a slight limp. He has no other history of medical or psychiatric illness. He says he used to drink one to two beers nightly but has been drinking two to three beers nightly for the past week. Physical examination confirms the previous gunshot injury to the calf and shows no other abnormalities. On mental status examination, he is irritable and says he is not depressed. He tells the physician, "They made me come. I'm not interested in talking with anyone. I just want to spend time with my buddies and be left alone." Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.A: Encourage the patient to discuss the trauma in detail
choices.B: Provide information about the range of reactions to trauma
choices.C: Recommend group therapy with other trauma survivors
choices.D: Recommend a 1-month medical leave of absence from active duty
choices.E: Recommend a physician-led trauma debriefing series

correctExplanation: This patient has had a recent exposure to trauma 1 week ago and is now experiencing emotional numbness, anhedonia, avoidance, and self-medication with alcohol. These findings suggest a diagnosis of acute stress disorder. Acute stress disorder presents similarly to post-traumatic stress disorder, with symptoms of intrusive thoughts, hyperarousal, dissociation, avoidance, and/or depressed mood. However, acute stress disorder presents within 1 month of a traumatic event whereas post-traumatic stress disorder lasts over a month beyond the event. It typically lasts between 3 days and 1 month. Pharmacotherapy is typically not indicated, but cognitive behavioral therapy may be helpful. In this case, providing information about the range of reactions to trauma will be most helpful as it will educate the patient and may prompt him to seek help for his symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Encouraging the patient to discuss the trauma in detail (Choice A) is not appropriate at this time. Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy is an effective therapy in treating acute stress disorder but does not include discussing the trauma in detail.

questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 27-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by his girlfriend because of a 6-week history of daily episodes of hearing a voice telling him that he is Christ. He is convinced that he has the power to heal the sick and requests that he be admitted into the wards to help the patients. During the past 4 weeks , he has had a 10-kg (22-lb) we ight loss. He has not slept more than 2 hours nightly for 2 weeks. When he is awake at night, he watches television or calls strangers on the telephone. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 80 kg (176 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m2. His tem perature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows no other abnormalities . On mental status examinat ion, he appears restless and agitated. He flirts with fema le staff members and tries to convince people of his powers. He has pressured speech and talks incessa ntly. There is no evidence of visual hallucinations. Recall is difficult to assess because he cannot concentrate. Long-term memory is intact. He is oriented to person, place, and time. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.C: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

correctExplanation: Bipolar disorder can be divided into two subtypes. Bipolar I disorder presents with episodes of mania and frequent ly includes hypomanic and depressive episodes. Bipolar II disorder, in contrast, always presents with hypomanic and depressive episodes, but no manic episodes. These episodes can transition from one to the other, or the patient can be euthymic between episodes. According to the DSM-5, mania is characterized by a persistently elevated or irritable mood with increased energy that lasts at least 1 week or requires hospitalization. It is accompanied by three or more of the following : increased self-esteem, decreased sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, psychomotor agitation or hyperactivity, and disinhibition or impulsivity (eg, gambling, unprotected sexual activity, frivolous spending). Delusions and hallucinations can also occur during manic episodes. Hypomanic episodes are similar to manic episodes but are less severe and do not markedly impair social functioning or require hospitalization. Depressive episodes can also occur with bipolar disorder and are classically characterized by depressed mood, anhedonia, excessive feelings of guilt, changes to sleep patterns (eg, sleeping too much or too little), decreased energy, poor concentration, decreased appetite, psychomotor slowing, and suicidal ideation. This patient is experiencing a manic episode with psychotic featu res based on auditory hallucinations, delusions of grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, psychomotor agitation, pressured speech, and flirtatious behavior, making bipolar disorder the likely diagnosis. Severe episodes require hospitalization and are treated with lithium, valproate, or an antipsychotic medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E.

questionStem: A 5-year-o ld boy has had temperatures to 38.9°C (102°F), cough, and coryza for 2 days and visual hallucinations of animals and people for 2 hours. His mother has been giving him an over-the-counter cold medicine for 24 hours, but it has not relieved his symptoms. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). Examination shows a clear nasal discharge. Which of the following is the most likely reason for the child's hallucinations?
correctExplanation: Dextromethorphan is a common ingredient in antitussive medications such as cough medicine. It antagonizes N-methyl-d-aspartate glutamate receptors and, when used in excess, has mild opioid effects and can act as a dissociative hallucinogen. Patients with toxicity can present with hallucinations, mania, panic, and agitation. Dextromethorphan can also cause adverse effects including nausea, vomiting, insomnia, mydriasis, fever, tachycardia, and sedation. Dextromethorphan should not be given to patients taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors because of its potentia l for severe interaction with resulting autonomic instability. Treatment is supportive, with restraint and sedation for agitation, cooling measures for hyperthermia, and fluids for rhabdomyolysis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Behaviora l abnormalities (Choice A) would not be an appropriate diagnosis, since there is likely a medical cause for this child's hallucinations. Behavioral disorders such as oppositional defiant disorder, autism spectrum disorder, or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder are not characterized by hallucinations and would not present acutely as in this patient. Hyperpyrexia (Choice C) can cause hallucinations in patients, but hyperpyrexia typically refers to hyperthermia greater than 41.0°C (106.0°F). This patient's degree of fever is within the expected range and would be unlikely to cause hallucinations. Increased intracrania l pressure (Choice D) can be caused by tumors, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis with impaired cerebrospina l fluid drainage, or other pathologies and can present with neurologic deficits, altered mental status, and seizures. Increased intracrania l pressure would be less likely to cause hallucinations. Neuronal inflammation (Choice E) such as in encepha litis can be caused by herpes simplex virus, which may present with fever, headache, seizures, focal neurologic signs, and confusion. Imaging may show inflammation in the tempora l lobe. Patients with encepha litis may hallucinate, but this is rare, and this patient's hallucinations are more likely caused by dextromethorphan.

questionStem: A 27-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after his brother found him agitated, tremulous, and complaining of a headac he. He had eaten a peanut butter sandwich 12 hours before his symptoms began. He has a 10-year history of severe major depressive disorder. During this period, he has attempted suicide three times despite treatment with both selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants. Eight days ago, he went to a new physician because of increasing despondency. This physician immediately discontinued the fluoxetine and substituted tranylcypromine to start 1 week later. He also instructed the patient to start a monoamine oxidase inhibitor diet immediately. Current medications a lso include diphenhydramine as needed for seasonal allergies. He has no history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or migraine. On arrival, he is agitated. His temperature is 40.6°C (105°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 180/120 mm Hg. Physical examination shows diaphoresis and tremor of the upper extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ bilaterally; there are no pathologic reflexes. On mental status examination, he is complaining of occipital headache. He is oriented to person but not to place or time. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOls), which are structura lly similar to biogenic amines, bind to monoamine oxidase and inhibit its enzymatic degradation of biogenic amines. This increases synaptic concentrations of serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. The MAOls are effective for depression and anxiety but are typical ly used only after other agents have failed because of the risk for serious adverse effects. The MAOls decrease the peripheral degradation of tyramine (a sympathomimetic biogenic amine that does not cross the blood-brain barrier), which may lead to hypertensive crisis if combined with dietary tyramine (eg, cheese, wine). Therefore, patients on MAOls must adhere to a low-tyramine diet. Combining MAOls with other serotonergic agents or starting MAOls within 2 weeks of discontinuing another serotonergic drug also increases the risk for serotonin syndrome. Serotonin syndrome, the result of serotonin toxicity, can lead to the triad of acute confusion, autonomic hyperactivity (hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypertension), and neuromuscular excitability (tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia). As a result of serotonin receptors in the gastrointestinal tract, vomiting and diarrhea can also occur. Management of serotonin syndrome includes discontinuation of all serotonergic agents (the MAOI in this case), supportive care of autonomic instability, sedation with benzodiazepines, intravenous fluid repletion, and cooling measures. Cyproheptadine is an antidote with nonspecific serotonin antagonist properties that can be used, but evidence of efficacy is mixed.

questionStem: A previo usly healt hy 27-year-o ld woma n comes to the physician because of a 2-mo nth history of crying spells, poor concentration, fatigue, and lethargy. She says that she sleeps at least 12 hours daily and is no longer interested in social izing. She recent ly broke up with her boyfriend of 10 months, and her work perfor mance has begun to decline; she is afra id that she will lose her job if it does not improve. She does not drink alcoho l or use illicit drugs. Menses occur at regular 28- to 30-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 2 wee ks ago. She has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight gain over the past 9 months. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. Physical exam ination shows no abnorma lities. Menta l status exam ination shows a sad mood and restricted affect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient meets criteria for major depressive disorder (MOD). Symptoms of MOD include 2 or more weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia (eg, decreased interest in socializing), guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, suicidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. Though neurovegetative symptoms typically manifest as decreased appetite and sleep, patients with a subtype of MOD called atypical depression experience hyperphagia and hypersomno lence. Patients with atypical depression may possess an increased symptom burden and an increased risk for suicide. The most effective treatment includes both psychotherapy and antidepressant medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adjustment disorder with depressed mood (Choice A) refers to the onset of disproportionate distress within 3 months of an identifiable stressor with associated depressive symptoms that do not meet the diagnostic criteria for MOD. This patient meets the diagnostic criteria of MOD. Dysthymic disorder (Choice B), more commonly known as persistent depressive disorder, refers to depressive symptoms lasting longer than 2 years. Patients with dysthymic disorder do not meet MOD criteria. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice C) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. Though this patient is appropriately afraid she will lose her job, she does not demonstrate disproportionate anxiety symptoms.

questionStem: A 15-yea r-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his two friends because of unusual behav ior that began at a party 1 hour ago. His friends say that he became raucous and made an unwanted sexua l advance to a girl he had just met. He then ran into the street, careless to oncoming cars, saying he was able to avoid them. His pulse is 84/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. He is agitated when left alone, but he calms down when spoken to by nursing staff. Physical examination shows an unsteady gait. Pupils are equal and reactive . Which of the following is the most likely drug taken?
correctExplanation: Alcohol is the most likely substance that the patient has ingested. Alcoho l is metabolized by zero order kinetics in the liver by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase. Individuals with infrequent alcohol use are at greater risk for developing classic symptoms of alcohol intoxication including emotional !ability, disinhibition, slurred speech, ataxia, and even coma and blackouts. Clinical findings often demonstrate an alcohol scent on the breath, normally reactive pupils, slurring of speech, gait instability, slow respirations, frequent urination, and behavioral disturbances. Loss of inhibition is a feature of many drugs but is particular ly common with alcohol consumption. Treatment should focus on maintaining a safe environment, protecting the patient and others from harm , and monitoring and managing the patient's airway and breathing in the event of emesis, oversedation, or coma. Treatment should also include supporting hydration and, in cases of chronic or severe intoxication, repleting any deficient vitamins and electrolytes. questionStem: A previous ly healthy 57-year-old woman comes to the physician with her husband because of an 8-week history of progressive confusion and memory loss. correctExplanation: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a human prion disease in which prion proteins replicate throughout the brain and cause neurotoxicity. Stimulus-induced myoclonus is a specific sign of CJD. Over time, the dementia rapidly progresses, invariab ly leading to death within a year. A probable CJD diagnosis can be made clinically, though an autopsy showing spongiform degeneration of the cortex confirms the diagnosis. An EEG showing repetitive, periodic epileptiform discharges supports the diagnosis. Treatment is supportive (eg, hospice evaluation, education, benzodiazepines for myoclonus).

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld man is brought to the physician because of a change in personality over the past 4 months. He has become sexually disinhibited, tactless, impulsive, and easily irritated. Bulimia nervosa involves cycles of uncontrollable eating and compensatory behaviors that occur at least once a week over 3 months or more. These patients typically have a normal BMI. Patients that use vomiting as their purging behavior, in either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, may additional ly have signs of dental erosion, knuckle abrasions, hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Treatment of disorders is through a combined medical and psychiatric approach and involves corre,cting fluid and electrolyte derangements alongside behavioral and pharmacologic therapy. Additional ly, both disorders can be accompanied by major depression or generalized anxiety disorder. This patient continues to eat full meals, has a normal and consistent weight percentile, does not exercise excessively, and does not show signs of depression or anxiety. Her other behavioral changes are consistent with normal adolescent development (eg, disorganization, preferring time with friends over time with parents).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Recommending individual psychotherapy (Choice B) would be appropriate in the setting of anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, major depression, or generalized anxiety disorder. However, this patient is experiencing normal development. Recommending nutritional counseling (Choice C) may be useful if this patient decides to pursue a vegetarian diet, so that she and her family can ensure that she is obtaining all the correct nutrients. It can also be useful in the overall treatment plan of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa. Recommending that the father keep a log of what his daughter eats (Choice D) is not necessary. While this may be recommended for a patient with an eating disorder, this patient is taking in enough calories since she has maintained a consistent weight percentile and thus does not need to log her intake. This patient has remained consistent for a year and she is not displaying any signs of an eating disorder. Educationa l Objective: Changes to eating patterns and social interactions occur commonly in adolescence. While most changes are benign and only require reassurance, there are some disorders that require intervention. Bulimia nervosa involves cycles of uncontrollable eating and compensatory behaviors, and both disorders require a combined medical and psychiatric approach to treatment.

questionStem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after injuring her right arm. This is her third visit to the emergency department in 6 months. The parents say that she fell. The child is too upset to say how she injured herself. Her parents note that she is overly aggressive in day care, where she is not respond ing to instructio ns, and has hit other children. During her previous visit for a wrist injury, an x-ray of the wrist showed normal findings. On examination, the child appears fearful of the examiner, provides limited responses, and is restless and easily distracted. An x-ray of the right humerus shows a closed fracture. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Risk factors for child abuse include unstable family situations, prior history of abuse, major birth defects, and parental depression. Child abuse should be suspected when children present repeatedly for several injuries, and especially when the location, severity, pattern, or history are inconsistent with the reported mechanism. While toddlers typically demonstrate occasional defiance, and cooperative play is not expected to develop until 4 years of age, this child's aggressive behavior toward other children at daycare is abnormal and raises suspicion for abuse. Fractures that suggest intentional injury include rib fractures, metaphyseal corner fractures, long bone fractures, and certain skull fractures, or any fracture or bruising sustained in an area or location that could not be reasonably expected on the basis of the child's normal ambulatory and play habits. For example, a femur fracture would never be typical in a nonambulatory 6- month-old patient. If child abuse is suspected, child protective services should be contacted immediately.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Admitting this patient into the hospital (Choice A) would not be immediately medically necessary. However, after a child protective services evaluation of the patient, the patient may need admission for further evaluation for child abuse and social services. Cognitive behavior therapy (Choice B) is a form of psychosocial therapy that focuses on challenging harmful thought s, beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors and developing coping strategies. Therapy may be necessary for the patient or parents at a later time but is not the next immediate step in management. ...

questionStem: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-year history of increasingly freque nt episodes of eye blinking and facial grimacing during the past 6 months that now occur severa l times daily. He also frequently makes grunting and throat-clea ring noises . His teacher often sends him out of the room for being disruptive. He says that he will repeatedly shrug one of his shoulders and attempt to hide this behav ior by smoothing his hair. He is embarrassed by these behav iors and can suppress them with effort, but they often return when he is distracted and are exacerbated by stress. The behaviors do not occur during sleep. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medicat ions. During the examination, he has severa l episodes of rapid, forceful eye blinking and throat clear ing. Physical exam ination shows no other abnormalities. Mental status examinat ion shows a mildly anxious mood and affect. Which of the following is the most appropr iate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Tourette disorder is a neurologic condition characterized by the presence of both motor and phonic tics that manifest in childhood or adolescence. Motor tics often include blinking, grimacing, shrugging, or neck movements. Phonic tics often include throat clearing, grunting, sniffing, or other comp lex vocalizations such as echolalia or coprola lia. Patients often experience a premonitory sensation or urge prior to the expression of the tic that is relieved by the tic's expression. Patients are typically able to suppress the expression of the tic for a period of time , although with significant effort. Treatment often requires a combined approach with pharmacologic therapy and behavioral training. First-line treatment includes antipsychotic medications such as aripiprazole, fluphenazine, haloperidol, or risperidone, though many medications can be appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dextroamphetamine (Choice A) and methylphenidate (Choice E) are both central nervous system stimulants that are useful for the treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). While ADHD often co-occurs, treatment with stimulants is not first-line since studies have found that these agents worsen tics. Hydroxyzine (Choice B) is a histamine inverse agonist that is useful for the treatment of pruritus, urticaria, and motion sickness. It is not typical ly used for the treatment of Tourette disorder. . .. -. - . - -..

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman, whose husband died 18 months ago, is admitted to the hospita l because of severe headac hes for 4 weeks. She is quiet and seems sad. She believes that she has brain cancer, deserves to be punished for her sins, and is being punished by God for past misdeeds. She has had fatigue and a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss over the past 4 months. Physical and neurologic examinat ions show no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Adjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct

correctExplanation: Major depressive disorder is the most likely diagnosis. Symptoms of major depressive disorder (MOD) typica lly include 2 or more weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, suicida l thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. The presence of somatic symptoms such as headache or gastrointestinal distress are also commonly seen in conjunction with depression. Additiona lly, this patient's delusion that she is being punished by God is consistent with a potentia lly accompanying psychotic feature without meeting criteria for schizoaffective disorder. While feelings of guilt and depressed mood are common within the first few months after the death of a loved one, these symptoms typically resolve and do not interfere with daily functioning. She should be assessed for the presence of suicidality and should be started on pharmacotherapy for her depression.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adjustment disorder with mixed disturbances of emotions and conduct (Choice A) describes a reaction to a known stressor that occurs within 3 months and presents with a combination of features including depressed mood, anxiety, and abnormal behavior not meeting criteria for a major depressive episode or bipolar disorder. This patient's husband died 18 months ago. Delusional disorder (Choice B) presents with fixed delusions in the absence of other psychiatric symptoms such as hallucinations, disorganization, depression, or mania. Schizophrenia (Choice D) presents with delusions, hallucinations, profound negative symptoms, or disorganized speech or behavior lasting for 6 months, not secondary to substance use, and contributing to profound dysfunction in everyday life. This patient does not meet criteria. Additiona lly, it is uncommon for older adults to deve lop this disorder.

questionStem: A 23-year-o ld man is brought to the phys ician by his mother because of increasing conflict between the two of them over the past 6 months. She says that he has become more difficult because of his growing concern about neighbors who he believes abuse the welfare system. He says that he has had specia l abilities to predict the future since the age of 15 years, but no one in his fam ily believes him. His mother says that he has never had many friends and descr ibes him as a loner. He has not used any drugs. He has not felt sad or depressed and has had no recent change in appetite or sleep disturbances. Physica l exam ination shows no abnorma lities. His language is vague and stilted. Wh ich of the following is the most likely persona lity disorder in this patient?
correctExplanation: Schizotypal persona lity disorder is one of the cluster A personality disorders, the odd or eccentric cluster. The disorder is characterized by odd behavior and thinking and a constricted affect. Patients with schizotypal personality disorder may have strange, overly metaphorica l or magical thinking, though they fluctuate in the degree of their conviction about these beliefs (which differentiates these beliefs from the fixed delusions of schizophrenia). The strange beliefs may also manifest as eccentric appearance. Patients may experience somatosensory illusions or other abnormal perceptions. Patients with schizotypal persona lity disorder may appear to lack interest in cultivating relationships and, because of an inability to interpret others' motivations, may be deeply distrustful and anxious around others. Personality disorders are persistently maladaptive ways of relating to the self and to society that typical ly appear by early adulthood.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Antisocial persona lity disorder (Choice A) is a cluster B personality disorder, the emotional or dramatic cluster, that arises from a deficit in empathy, resulting in pervasive violations of others' rights, aggression, and a hostile and manipulative attitude toward others.
