questionStem: A homeless 27-year-old man who is being treated with antipsychotic and antiparkinson ian drugs comes to the emergency department because he feels anxious and has difficulty urinating. He reports seeing visions. He is hyperactive and disoriented to time and place and has difficulty focusing on nearby objects. Physical examinat ion shows dry mouth, flushed skin, and tachycardia at rest. There is no evidence of muscular rigidity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.D: Noncompl iance with antipsychotic drug therapy

correctExplanation: Acetylcholine activity in the brain mediates attention and motivation. Anticholinergic agents commonly cause cognitive impairment or delirium. This patient's antiparkinsonian medications are likely anticholinergic agents (eg, benztropine, diphenhydramine) utilized to prevent the extrapyramidal adverse effects of antipsychotic medications. Along with cognitive impairment (leading to this patient's disorientation), anticholinergic effects can include hallucinations, sedation, ataxia, visual disturbances (cycloplegia, or loss of accommodation), dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, constipation, and flushed skin. In patients demonstrating impairing anticholinergic toxicity, anticholinergic medications should be discontinued.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. An extrapyramida l syndrome (Choice B) may result from antipsychotic medication use. Patients typically present with acute dystonic reaction, parkinsonism, and/or akathisia without significant disorientation. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (Choice C) is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. Dry mouth, flushed skin, difficulty urinating, and vision abnormalities would be atypical. Noncompliance with antipsychotic drug therapy (Choice D) and psychosis due to substance abuse (Choice E) could result in increased hallucinations and/or delusions. Disorientation, dry mouth, flushed skin, difficulty urinating, and vision abnorma lities would be atypical. Educational Objective: Anticholinergic agents (eg, diphenhydramine, benztropine) common ly cause cognitive impairment, hallucinations, sedation, ataxia, visual disturbances (cycloplegia, or loss of accommodation), dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, constipation, and flushed skin. Offending medications should be discontinued.

questionStem: A 24-year-o ld woman comes to the phys ician with her husba nd because of an 8-year history of increasing dayt ime fatigue . She says that she has difficulty remaining awake whenever she sits down to relax. She has never been able to drive more than 30 minutes without becomi ng so sleepy that she needs to pull the car over and stop. Her husband says that once every 2 months, she gets up in the middle of the night and does not respo nd when he calls her name . He says that she does not snore. The patient repo rts that in high schoo l she trained herself not to laugh because she felt weak and could not rema in stand ing after her friends told jokes . She has no history of serious illness. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examinat ion, she appears concerned and has a reactive affect. She is alert and oriented to person, place, and time . Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.A: Keeping a sleep log for 2 weeks

correctExplanation: Polysomnography is likely to confirm the diagnosis of narcolepsy in this patient. Narcolepsy common ly presents with hypnagogic hallucinations, daytime somnolence, sleep hallucinations, and cataplexy (muscle weakness triggered by strong emotions). The pathogenesis of narco lepsy involves the loss of orexin-A and orexin-B, which are neurotransmitters found primari ly in the hypothalamus that promote wakefulness and inhibit rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Loss of these neurotransmitters permits abnormal transition from wakefulness to REM sleep with the consequent development of hallucinations and other features of narco lepsy, including cataplexy and sleep paralysis. Diagnosis can be made in patients with daytime somnolence and cataplexy or, in cases where cataplexy is not present, with polysomnography. Polysomnography is a sleep study performed using specialized equipment to measure oxygenation, end-tida l carbon dioxide, and time spent in various sleep stages. Patients with narcolepsy demonstrate decreased sleep latency and rapid entry into REM sleep. Other findings include spontaneous awakening and long stretches of light, non-REM sleep. Pharmacotherapy is directed as promoting wakefu lness and avoiding catap lexy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Keeping a sleep log for 2 weeks (Choice A) can be helpfu l for patients who are suspected to have poor sleep hygiene and is used to identify behaviors that may be contributing to poor sleep. It is typically used for patients with insomnia, not excessive sleepiness. MRI of the brain (Choice B) is an unnecessary diagnostic test that is unlikely to provide any meaningful information about this patient's condition. This patient has no focal neurologic deficits and no other symptoms of neurologic disease.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman with schizoaffect ive disorder is brought to the emergency department because of a ?-day history of progress ive lethargy, loss of appetite, nausea, and leg swelling; she has had jaund ice since this morning. Five weeks ago, she was hospitalized for treatme nt of her psychiatric symptoms. Treatme nt with three medicat ions was started during hospita lization, but she does not remem ber their names . She has no history of liver disease or other serious illness. She appears drowsy. Her pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 105/70 mm Hg. There is scleral icterus. Abdomina l examinat ion shows tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Neurologic examination shows a fine bilateral hand tremor. Mental status examination shows no evidence of hallucinations or delusions. She is oriented to person, place, and year but not to the day of the week or month. Serum studies show: Bilirubin, total 5 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L AST 240 U/L ALT 210 U/L Which of the following medicat ions is most likely responsible for these findings?
correctExplanation: Valproic acid is the medication that is most likely responsib le for this patient's findings. Valproic acid is an anti-epileptic drug and mood stabilizer that is occasiona lly used to treat patients with schizoaffective or bipolar disorder. Inadvertent or intentiona l overdose can lead to a number of clinical syndromes, such as hyperammonemia leading to encepha lopathy, hepatotoxicity with increased AST and ALT, and cerebral edema with coma. This patient's mental status and tremor may be the result of hyperammonemia, which occurs as a result of accumulation of propionic acid, a metabolite of valproic acid that prevents processing of ammonia through the urea cycle. It is often associated with mildly increased liver enzymes. While rare, acute fulminant hepatotoxicity can occur as a result of valproic acid overdose. Because of this, the patient should undergo additiona l evaluation of the prothrombin time or INR to assess for coagu lopathy. Frequently, hepatotoxicity is self-limited and is treated supportive ly and with remova l of the offending drug.

questionStem: A 29-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of the inability to maintain an erection throug h completion of sexual activity. He has been married for 3 months and has not been able to complete coitus over the past 2 months. He is usually able to attain an erect ion by direct penile stimulat ion and is often aware of nocturnal erections when waking during the night. For the past month, he and his wife have attempted to have intercourse about twice a week. He drinks several alcoho lic beverages before engaging in sexual activity i n an effort to relax . He has had two major depressive episodes over the past 4 years and was successfully treated with desipramine; he has not taken the medication since his marriage. questionStem: A ?-year-o ld boy is brought to the physician by his adoptive parents because of ongoing concern about his behavior and academic performance. He is two grade levels behind his peers in reading and frequently has fights with other children. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His biological mother abused multiple substances before and during pregnancy. On adoption at the age of 15 months, there was some evidence that she may have physical ly abused him. He is at the 10th percentile for height and 5th percenti le for weight. His pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 116/78 mm Hg. Examination shows a flattened nasal bridge, a long philtrum, and prominent ears. During the interview, he is friendly but becomes frustrated and distracted and is unable to sit still. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Alcohol is a proven teratogen, as alcohol use during pregnancy leads to irreversible fetal neurologic effects and physical malformations in a cluster of symptoms called fetal alcohol syndrome. Fetal alcohol syndrome is a leading cause of intellectual disability in the United States and would explain this patient's poor academic performance. As a result of the failure of cell migration, fetal alcohol syndrome also presents with physical abnormalities such as microcephaly, facial abnormalities (small palpebral fissures, thin vermilion border, cleft lip/palate, smooth or long philtrum), limb deformities, and congenital heart disease. Patients with fetal alcohol syndrome may demonstrate abnormal bone development (eg, cervical spine fusion) and delayed bone growth. Though substance use during pregnancy can result in obstetric complications such as preterm birth, the physical malformations, as those seen in this case, are specific to alcohol use.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Angelman syndrome (Choice A) occurs in patients who have paternal disomy (who have inherited both copies of a chromosome from the biological father rather than one copy from each parent) of chromosome 15. Angelman syndrome is characterized by short stature, intellectua l disability, severe speech impairment, and ataxia. The facial features present in this case are more likely secondary to fetal alcohol syndrome. Fragile X syndrome (Choice C) is an X-linked dominant cause of inherited intellectual disability that presents as a result of a CGG­ trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene. It presents with clinical features including intellectual disability, an elongated face with a prominent jaw, a high-arched palate, large ears, hyperextensible joints, and postpubertal macroorchidism. This patient's birth history and constellation of physical features suggest fetal alcohol syndrome instead.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of increasingly severe pain that originates in her left shoulder and radiates to her elbow. She describes the pain as constant and burning, rating her current pain as a 7 on a 10-point scale. Eighteen months ago, she sustained a nerve injury of the left upper extremity in a motor vehicle collision. Since that time, she has been unable to return to work. Current medications include oxycodone and gabapentin. Physical examination shows atrophy of the left thenar eminence. Muscle strength in the left forearm and finger flexors is 3/5. On sensory examination, there is severe pain with light stroking of the antero lateral aspect of the left arm. Further sensory testing is deferred. During the examination she tells her physician, "I'm tired of all this. My medicat ion is not strong enough. It only takes the edge off my pain, which is only getting worse. I'm realizing I'll be like this foreve r." Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?
